2107329463914471604.a:
Resversatrol Deficiency in the Diet
@BrianRoemmele

c-Myb (MYB)
In natural killer (NK) cells, resveratrol raises c-Myb mRNA and protein through Akt and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2), downstream of PTEN and S6K1. c-Myb is required for the effect: a c-Myb inhibitor (celastrol) or c-Myb knockdown blocks resveratrol-driven NK activation when combined with IL-2. That is a direct functional link in immune cells, reported in International Journal of Molecular Sciences (2020).

Separately, plant R2R3-MYB factors (VviMYB14 and VviMYB15 in grapevine) activate stilbene synthase genes and thereby control resveratrol biosynthesis. Those are plant MYBs, not human c-MYB.

HDAC2
Resveratrol intersects HDAC2 in several ways, with direction depending on the model:

Enzymatic inhibition. In vitro profiling and docking studies show resveratrol can inhibit class I, II, and IV HDACs, including HDAC2, in a dose-dependent manner (for example in hepatoblastoma cells and nuclear extracts). Concentrations used are often high (tens of micromolar). Derivatives built on a resveratrol scaffold have been optimized as more selective HDAC1/HDAC2 inhibitors.
Protein-level downregulation. In prostate cancer cells, resveratrol lowers MTA1, MTA2, MTA3, HDAC1, and HDAC2 and disrupts the MTA1/HDAC1/2 unit of the NuRD complex, which increases PTEN acetylation and restrains Akt.
Context-dependent restoration. In cigarette-smoke emphysema models, resveratrol increased HDAC2 (and glucocorticoid receptor) expression and restored corticosteroid sensitivity, the opposite of simple inhibition.
Resveratrol is also a well-known activator of the NAD+-dependent class III deacetylase SIRT1. Class I enzymes such as HDAC2 are zinc-dependent and are not the same as sirtuins, so both “HDAC inhibition” and “SIRT1 activation” can occur and should not be conflated.
